title: AI and the Future of ELT

pts: Conversational AI offers learners essentially unlimited, patient, low-stakes speaking and writing practice outside class time.
This connects to Unit 56's advanced-autonomy work — AI tools substantially expand what self-directed practice can look like.
Access and quality vary considerably, and this remains a fast-developing, not yet fully settled, area of practice.

v: 20 minutes at home or in a lab; 10 minutes in class
A device with a chatbot; a printed role card; a reflection slip

items: Give learners a role card with a scenario, for example booking a bus ticket from Bengaluru to Mangaluru.
Provide a ready-made prompt that sets the AI’s role, the learner’s level and the length of its replies.
Learners complete the conversation, by typing or by voice, and save or copy it.
Learners underline one phrase they learned and one moment when they struggled.
In class, pairs repeat the role-play face to face without the AI and compare the two experiences.
Learners without devices practise with a printed ‘AI script’ prepared by the teacher, then role-play with a partner.
Support: ask the AI to use short sentences and give two answer choices each turn.
Challenge: ask the AI to introduce a problem (the bus is full) that the learner must solve.

blocks.x: A structured prompt (written for this book):

lines: You are a ticket clerk at a bus station in Bengaluru. I am a learner of English at A2 level. Speak in short, simple sentences. Ask me one question at a time. If I make a mistake, continue the conversation, and at the end list up to three corrections.
A: Good morning. Where would you like to go?
B: I want go to Mangaluru tomorrow.
A: Certainly. What time would you like to travel?

blocks.x: The prompt keeps the AI patient and at the learner’s level. The face-to-face repeat in class keeps the human interaction at the centre.

body: Purpose: to show AI as a practice partner, not a teacher. Content: a learner at home with a phone showing a simple chat; a thought bubble shows the same learner later talking with a classmate; a small caption reads ‘practise, then perform’. Style: warm, realistic. Board version: a phone outline with two speech bubbles, arrow to two stick figures.

items: ChatGPT, Google Gemini, Microsoft Copilot and Claude (each with a free tier and paid plans; age requirements and features vary) [VERIFY current terms and age limits].

blocks.x: A printed dialogue script and cue cards for pair role-play.

pts: AI tools can give fast, patient feedback on discrete grammar and vocabulary points, extending Unit 18's earlier automated-feedback discussion.
Genuine communicative appropriacy and nuanced pragmatic judgement remain harder for current tools to assess reliably.
The balance between AI-assisted and human feedback continues to shift as the technology develops.

v: Three learner paragraphs (with consent, anonymized); AI access

items: Take three anonymized learner paragraphs.
Write your own feedback on each.
Ask an AI tool for feedback using a clear prompt.
Compare the two sets under four headings: grammar and vocabulary, organization, appropriacy and tone, and encouragement.
Decide which kinds of feedback you will delegate to AI and which you will keep.
Learners compare AI feedback with peer feedback (Unit 43) on their own drafts.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

blocks.x: Learner sentence (written for this book): Respected sir, I am writing to complain about the bad roads, kindly do the needful immediately.

lines: AI feedback: corrected the comma splice; suggested please take action for do the needful.

Teacher feedback: noted the comma splice, and also that do the needful is a familiar Indian English formula; discussed with the learner whether the reader is local or international and what tone suits a complaint.

blocks.x: The AI caught the grammar. The teacher’s feedback addressed audience, variety (Unit 74) and pragmatic choice, which remain harder for tools to judge reliably.

body: Purpose: to compare the strengths of AI and teacher feedback. Content: one learner paragraph with two sets of annotations, one in a mechanical font along the lines (grammar marks), one in handwriting in the margins (questions about audience and tone). Style: clean, realistic. Board version: a paragraph with two colours of underlining.

items: Write & Improve from Cambridge (free) for automated writing feedback [VERIFY current features].
Grammarly (free plan; paid Premium).

blocks.x: Peer-feedback checklists and teacher comments on paper.

body: When you ask an AI for feedback, tell it the learner’s level and the task’s purpose, and ask it to limit corrections to three. Unlimited correction overwhelms learners, just as it does when a teacher marks every error (Unit 8).

points.sub: A new tool for an old craft
pts: AI tools can accelerate aspects of the materials-writing process introduced in Unit 69, from drafting to generating varied practice items.
Human judgement remains essential for pedagogical soundness, cultural appropriateness, and genuine learner-fit.
This is best understood as augmenting, not replacing, the materials-design skill this series has built.

v: AI access; a materials checklist from Unit 69

items: Ask an AI tool to draft a short reading text and five questions for a specific class and topic.
Check the draft against a checklist: level, accuracy of facts, cultural fit, representation, question quality and learner interest.
Rewrite at least three parts.
Record the time saved and the time spent correcting.
Share the final version and the checklist results with a colleague.
Use AI only for the parts of materials writing that are most mechanical, such as generating varied gap-fill sentences.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

blocks.x: An AI-drafted text about a village fair, checked by a teacher:

lines: Level: several sentences too long for A2; shortened.
Facts: the text placed a Kannada festival in the wrong season; corrected.
Representation: all characters were boys; changed to a mixed group.
Questions: four of five were literal recall; two replaced with inference questions.

blocks.x: Human judgement remained essential for pedagogical soundness and cultural appropriateness. AI augmented the craft of Unit 69; it did not replace it.

body: Purpose: to show AI drafts as raw material for teacher judgement. Content: a teacher at a desk with an AI-generated draft covered in handwritten corrections and a checklist beside it with ticks and crosses. Style: realistic, warm. Board version: a page with marks and a checklist.

items: Any general-purpose AI chatbot (free tiers available) for drafting.
Canva for Education (free for teachers) for layout.

blocks.x: Adapt existing coursebook texts using the same checklist.

pts: AI-assisted scoring can support the reliability challenges raised in Unit 21 and Unit 46, alongside genuine new validity questions.
Automated essay scoring in particular raises real, actively debated questions about what such systems actually measure.
This connects directly to the ethical questions around AI in assessment addressed later in this tier (Unit 99).

v: Two learner essays (written for this book); a short reading on automated scoring

items: Review validity and reliability from Units 21 and 46.
Present two essays: one short but thoughtful, one long and fluent but off-topic.
Ask groups to predict which would score higher with an automated system that relies on features such as length, vocabulary range and error counts.
Discuss what the system would and would not measure.
List questions to ask before any automated scoring is used for decisions about learners.
Participants test a free automated feedback tool with the two essays and compare its judgements with their own [VERIFY tool terms before uploading learner work].
Support: provide a list of features that automated systems commonly use.
Challenge: participants read Xi (2010) and summarize its main questions.

blocks.x: Questions to ask about automated scoring:

lines: What features does it use, and do they match the construct (for example, argument quality)?
Has it been checked for bias against particular varieties of English, such as Indian English?
Who reviews scores, and can learners appeal?
Is it used for feedback (lower stakes) or decisions (higher stakes)?

blocks.x: Automated scoring can support reliability, but Xi (2010) argues that its validity must be demonstrated for each use. Unit 99 examines these ethical questions further.

body: Purpose: to show validity questions in automated scoring. Content: two essays fed into a machine; the long off-topic essay receives a higher score; a teacher looks at the result with a raised eyebrow. Style: lightly humorous. Board version: two boxes, arrow, machine, scores.

items: Write & Improve (free) as an example of automated feedback for learners.

blocks.x: A paper checklist of validity questions for school discussions.

pts: Negotiation of meaning (Unit 30), affective climate-building (Unit 22), and genuine cultural exchange (Unit 24) remain distinctly human classroom functions.
This series' consistent emphasis on interaction and relationship isn't diminished by AI's genuine, real capabilities elsewhere.
The most productive framing treats AI as a powerful tool within a still-human-centred practice, not a replacement for it.

items: Give groups cards naming classroom functions: explaining grammar, generating practice items, correcting spelling, noticing a learner is upset, building trust, negotiating meaning with a peer, sharing a festival tradition, and so on.
Groups sort them into ‘AI can help a lot’, ‘AI can help a little’ and ‘mainly human’.
Groups justify the ‘mainly human’ category with reference to Units 22, 24 and 30.
Discuss how to protect time for human functions in a timetable that may include AI.
Learners do a simplified version of the sort and discuss what they value in their teacher and classmates.
Support: provide examples for each category.
Challenge: groups identify functions whose category may change in five years and explain why.

lines: AI can help a lot: generating practice items, explaining a grammar rule again, spelling checks.
AI can help a little: feedback on organization, conversation practice.
Mainly human: noticing that Lakshmi is withdrawn today, building a supportive climate (Unit 22), negotiating meaning with a real partner (Unit 30), sharing the meaning of a family festival (Unit 24).
A: Can AI not have a conversation?
B: It can simulate one. But a classmate’s misunderstanding is real, and fixing it together is real learning.

body: Purpose: to show AI as a tool around a human-centred classroom. Content: concentric circles; at the centre, a teacher and learners in a circle labelled ‘relationship, interaction, culture’; in the outer ring, small AI icons labelled ‘practice’, ‘explanation’, ‘drafting’. Style: warm, clear. Board version: two circles with labels.

items: Mentimeter (free plan) for a quick class vote on categories.

blocks.x: Sorting cards and three columns on the board.

pts: Unit 18's digital-divide concern applies with even more force to unevenly distributed, often costly AI tools.
Institutional and policy decisions about AI access will significantly shape whether these tools narrow or widen existing educational inequities.
This connects directly to Unit 71's discussion of institutional language policy — AI adoption is itself becoming a policy question.

v: Teachers, head teachers or DIET faculty
A simple access survey (written for this book)

items: Survey learners anonymously: device access at home, whose device, data availability and time of use.
Tabulate results by class and, where appropriate, by gender and school location.
Identify which AI-based tasks would exclude some learners.
Plan alternatives: school-time access, shared devices, offline versions.
Share findings with the school management or at a DIET meeting as input to local policy (Unit 71 discusses language policy at institutional level).
Compare two schools in a cluster, one urban and one rural.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

points.h: Preparing Learners for an AI-Saturated World
pts: Learners increasingly need skill in using AI tools effectively and critically as part of their own language learning and future language use.
This connects to Unit 48's autonomy work — critical AI-tool evaluation is a natural extension of the resource-evaluation skill already taught there.
This is a genuinely new literacy this series' original framework didn't anticipate, worth explicit attention now.

items: Show three AI answers to learner questions, including one with an error.
Learners check each answer using a dictionary, a coursebook or a corpus.
Learners complete a checklist: accurate? level-appropriate? sources given? suitable for my purpose?
Discuss when to use AI, when to check it, and when not to use it (for example in assessed work where it is not allowed).
Learners write personal guidelines for AI use in their learning.
Link to learner autonomy (Unit 48): learners add AI to their resource-evaluation list.
Support: provide the corrections for comparison.
Challenge: learners improve a prompt to get a better answer, and explain why it worked.

blocks.x: An AI answer with an error (written for this book):

lines: Q: Is ‘I am knowing the answer’ correct?
AI: Yes, it is correct and natural in formal English.
S1: The coursebook says know is a state verb. We don’t use it in the continuous.
S2: But in Indian English people say it.
T: Good. So the AI was wrong about formal standard English, and you have also noticed a real difference between varieties (Unit 74). Always check.
Use AI to practise and to explain, but check important answers in a second source, and follow the rules for assessed work.

body: Purpose: to teach critical AI use. Content: a learner holding a phone showing an AI answer, with a magnifying glass in the other hand; a dictionary and a coursebook on the desk; a checklist beside them. Style: friendly, practical. Board version: a phone outline with a question mark and a tick list.

items: Cambridge Dictionary (free) and SkELL (free) for checking AI answers.

blocks.x: Printed AI outputs and dictionaries in class.

pts: Neither uncritical enthusiasm nor reflexive rejection serves learners well — informed, evidence-responsive engagement does.
This connects directly to Unit 67's action-research habit — trying, evaluating, and adjusting AI tool use in one's own specific context.
This stance mirrors this entire series' consistent approach: principled judgement over either blind adoption or blind resistance.

v: One AI tool; a teaching journal

items: Choose one AI use, such as speaking practice or feedback on drafts.
Write a focused question, for example ‘Does weekly AI role-play practice increase learners’ willingness to speak in class?’.
Collect simple evidence: a short learner survey, a count of volunteers, teacher notes.
Review after the term, as in the action-research cycle of Unit 67.
Decide to continue, adjust or stop, and share the result with colleagues.
Run the inquiry with colleagues in a cluster and compare results.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

blocks.x: A teacher’s journal entry (written for this book):

lines: Week 6: Twelve learners used the AI role-play at home. Volunteers in class rose from 8 to 13, but most of the new volunteers already had phones. Next step: offer lab time to learners without devices and see if the pattern holds.

blocks.x: The stance is neither enthusiastic nor alarmed. It is informed and responsive to evidence, which is how this book has approached every new tool and technique.

body: Purpose: to show an evidence-responsive stance towards AI. Content: a small cycle of three arrows labelled ‘try’, ‘check’ and ‘adjust’ around a phone icon; a teacher’s journal lies open beside it. Style: clean, calm. Board version: a circle with three arrows and labels.

items: Google Forms (free) for short learner surveys.

body: Choose one AI tool and one specific use for it this term. Write a one-sentence question about its effect, collect one simple kind of evidence each week, and decide at the end of term whether to keep, change or drop it.

dek: Unit 84 of 100: closing this stretch of deep dives by looking forward — the genuine opportunities and real, unresolved questions artificial intelligence raises for language teaching.

aims.x: Artificial intelligence is already in many learners’ pockets. A Class 10 learner in Hubballi can ask a chatbot to explain the passive voice, correct a paragraph or play the part of a railway clerk. A teacher can generate twenty comprehension questions in a minute. This unit looks at what AI can and cannot do for language teaching, and at the questions of quality, equity and professional judgement it raises. It does not predict the future; it offers a stance and a set of classroom procedures for trying, evaluating and adjusting AI use in your own context.
By the end of this unit you should be able to:

items: use conversational AI as a structured practice partner for speaking and writing;
evaluate AI feedback on learner writing and decide where human feedback remains essential;
use AI to draft materials and apply a checklist for pedagogical and cultural quality;
explain the main validity and fairness questions raised by automated scoring;
identify classroom functions that remain distinctly human;
analyse equity and access issues in AI adoption in your school or district;
teach learners to use AI tools critically as part of their language learning;
plan a small action-research cycle to evaluate one AI tool in your own context.

why: Why this matters. This shift is already underway, not hypothetical. Understanding both its real potential and its real limitations is now a core part of professional literacy.

background.x: Computers have been used in language teaching since the 1960s, and computer-assisted language learning (CALL) has a substantial research tradition (Chapelle 2001). Automated writing evaluation tools have given feedback on grammar and style for years, and researchers have long cautioned that such feedback is uneven and must be integrated into good teaching rather than replacing it (Warschauer and Ware 2006; Stevenson and Phakiti 2014). What changed from late 2022 onwards was the arrival of widely available generative AI: large language models that produce fluent text in response to prompts and can hold extended conversations.

Early commentary on tools such as ChatGPT identified clear opportunities for language learning, including conversation practice, explanation, feedback and materials generation, alongside real limitations, such as confident errors, uneven quality and questions of academic integrity (Kohnke, Moorhouse and Zou 2023). UNESCO’s guidance on generative AI in education calls for a human-centred approach, age-appropriate use, data protection and building the capacity of teachers (UNESCO 2023). Because the tools change quickly, any specific claim about capability or cost in this unit may date fast. Treat tool names and features here as examples, and check them.

For India, the questions are especially sharp. NEP 2020 recognizes the potential of emerging technologies, including AI, and proposes a National Educational Technology Forum to guide their use, while stressing equity and the digital divide (Ministry of Human Resource Development 2020). Government platforms such as DIKSHA provide free digital content, and Bhashini, a national language-technology initiative, works on translation and speech tools for Indian languages [VERIFY current scope]. Yet many learners share a single parent’s phone, data is costly, and many classrooms have no device at all. NCF 2023 reminds us that technology must serve pedagogy, not the reverse (NCERT 2023).

This unit connects to Unit 18 on digital tools, Unit 48 and Unit 56 on autonomy, Unit 69 on materials writing and Unit 67 on action research. Unit 93 returns to educational technology research, and Unit 99 examines the ethics of AI in language assessment in depth. The stance here is the one this book has taken throughout: principled, evidence-responsive judgement rather than enthusiasm or rejection.

items: Prompt design. A structured prompt for AI role-play at a given level, with evidence of learners using it.
Feedback comparison. A comparison of AI and teacher feedback on three texts, with decisions about what to delegate.
Access audit. A summary of device and data access in one class, with an inclusive plan.
AI inquiry report. A short report of a one-term inquiry into one AI tool, with evidence and a decision.
How do your learners already use AI? How do you know?
Which parts of your work could AI support, and which should it not?
Who in your class might be excluded by an AI-based task?
How will you know if an AI tool is helping learning rather than replacing it?
How would you explain your school’s approach to AI to parents?
What is your own stance towards AI in teaching, and what evidence could change it?

perm: AI-generated text may reproduce material from its training data. Check drafts for close similarity to published sources, and follow your institution’s and publisher’s policies on disclosing AI use in materials [VERIFY current policy].

All prompts, dialogues, survey items and journal entries are written for this book; class figures are fictional. Screenshots of ChatGPT, Gemini, Copilot, Claude, Write & Improve, Grammarly, Read Along or DIKSHA require permission or replacement with original illustrations. Learner writing must not be uploaded to AI tools without consent and a check of the tool’s data policy, and AI-generated materials should be disclosed according to institutional policy.

terms.def: The knowledge and skills needed to use artificial intelligence tools critically and responsibly, including understanding what they can and cannot do, checking their output, and recognizing issues of bias and academic honesty.
The use of software to assign scores to spoken or written performances; it raises questions of validity, fairness and transparency, especially when the scores inform important decisions.
Software that analyses learners’ writing and provides scores or feedback on features such as grammar, vocabulary and organization; it is most useful as a supplement to teacher and peer feedback.
The extent to which a test measures the construct it claims to measure, and not other abilities; for example, whether a writing score reflects writing rather than typing speed.
The gap between those who have access to digital devices, the internet and the skills to use them and those who do not.

Artificial intelligence that produces new text, images or audio in response to prompts, such as chatbots based on large language models. It offers teaching possibilities but can produce confident errors.
An approach to AI in education that keeps human agency, wellbeing and teacher judgement at the centre, with attention to data protection and age-appropriate use (UNESCO 2023).

A generative AI system trained on vast amounts of text to predict and produce fluent language in response to prompts, such as ChatGPT; useful for practice and materials, but it can produce confident errors that teachers must check.
1. In error correction, a move that pushes the learner to self-correct, such as a clarification request or metalinguistic clue. 2. In generative AI, the instruction or question typed to the system.
